extracted.intended_audience: school administrators, athletic directors, higher-education counsel, compliance officers, and other stakeholders in education and sports law
extracted.subtask_description: A legal news/alert summarizing the Department of Education's withdrawal of a proposed rule on athletic-team participation by gender identity, describing the remaining legal standards (34 C.F.R. §106.41), prior guidance, and related congressional and procedural developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE proposed-rule standard for sex-related athletic criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: If a recipient adopted or applied sex-related criteria that would limit or deny a student’s eligibility to participate on a team consistent with their gender identity, such criteria must be substantially related to the achievement of an important educational objective and minimize harms to students whose opportunity to participate on a team consistent with their gender identity would be limited or denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the substantive test set forth in the Department's April 13, 2023 proposed rule; it attracted more than 150,000 public comments during a 30-day period and was later withdrawn by the Department on Dec. 26, 2024.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply longstanding 34 C.F.R. § 106.41 framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will continue to apply the longstanding legal standards set forth in 34 CFR 106.41 when it receives complaints of discrimination regarding an alleged failure to provide equal opportunity to participate in athletics regardless of sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under §106.41, a recipient is prohibited from discriminating on the basis of sex with respect to providing athletic programs or activities, may provide sex-segregated teams for competitive activities or contact sports, and must provide equal athletic opportunity for members of both sexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of sex-segregated teams (competitive/contact sports)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.41 permits a recipient to provide sex-segregated teams for competitive activities or contact sports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting sex-segregated teams is allowed but must be balanced with the broader §106.41 obligation to provide equal athletic opportunity; the Department will apply this framework in complaint investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: OGC 2021 guidance on separation by biological sex (Bostock context)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of the General Counsel guidance stated that if a recipient chooses to provide 'separate teams for members of each sex … then it must separate those teams solely on the basis of biological sex, male or female, and not on the basis of transgender status or sexual orientation, to comply with Title IX.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This guidance was issued in January 2021 in the aftermath of Bostock v. Clayton County; the alert notes that such guidance could be reinstated under a returning Trump administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional proposal to amend Title IX definition of 'sex' and ban transgender athletes
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed bill (fast-tracked as part of a rules package) would add language to Title IX making it a violation for a recipient to 'permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women,' and would define 'sex' solely as 'a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in a rules package agreed by Congress on Jan. 3, 2025; represents a possible statutory change that would alter how institutions must apply Title IX in athletics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking procedural factors: public comment period and litigation influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department received more than 150,000 responses during the 30-day public comment period for the proposed rulemaking; multiple pending lawsuits related to Title IX’s application to athletic eligibility criteria were also outstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural elements (extensive public comment and active litigation) were cited as reasons for withdrawing and terminating the rulemaking proceeding; they illustrate that litigation risk and comment volume can affect agency rulemaking outcomes.
